title: A Systematic Analysis of Out-of-Distribution Detection Under Representation and Training Paradigm Shifts
claim: Which detector families are statistically competitive depends systematically on representation and training paradigm, with distinct patterns across shift regimes.
layout: 4 panels left-to-right sharing rows; dot-and-line columns on shaded bands, dotted top-3 boxes
description: Four side-by-side dot-matrix panels titled ConfidNet (Vanilla CE), DeVries, Deep Gamblers and ViT (finetune). Each panel is a grid. Rows are 22 confidence scoring functions (REN, PE, MSR, Energy, NNGuide, CTM, Residual and others). Columns are source dataset to regime pairs, such as cifar10->test, cifar100->near and tinyimagenet->far. The upper rows sit on a lavender band for head-side scores, and the lower rows sit on a yellow band for feature-side scores. In each column, colored dots mark the top-clique members and are joined by curved vertical lines. Green is test, blue is near, red is mid and orange is far. Dotted rectangles outline the three most frequent winners per panel. A legend runs along the bottom. The eye goes first to the colored connected dots and the dotted boxes, which show how winners move between bands and panels.
caption: Top-clique maps across four training settings (AURC/AUGRC, α = 0.05, 22 CSFs). Panels, left to right: VGG-13 with vanilla cross-entropy (the ConfidNet paradigm of Section 3.1), VGG-13 with DeVries, VGG-13 with Deep Gamblers, and a fine-tuned ViT. Columns within each panel are the four source datasets crossed with the four evaluation regimes (test, near, mid, far); connected colored dots within a column show the Conover top clique. Rows are the filtered set of CSFs, grouped by where the score reads from the network: head-side scores (logit/softmax statistics, blue band) on top and feature-side scores (penultimate-feature geometry, peach band) on the bottom. Within each band, rows are ordered by regime centre-of-mass (near-dominant at top, far-dominant at bottom). Dotted rectangles mark the CSFs with the three highest clique counts per paradigm, including ties.
abstract: We present a systematic benchmark of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection confidence scoring functions (CSFs) through a representation-centric lens. Our study spans CNN and ViT backbones, multiple training paradigms, four image-classification source datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SuperCIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet), and OOD datasets grouped into near, mid, and far regimes based on CLIP-derived semantic distances. To compare CSFs across these settings, we employ a rank-based pipeline of Friedman and Conover tests that identifies top cliques of statistically indistinguishable winners under threshold-free ranking metrics (AURC and AUGRC). The main empirical finding is that the family of CSFs that are competitive detectors correlates with characteristics of the learned representation. For both CNNs and ViTs, simple probabilistic scores dominate misclassification detection. On CNNs, margin-based scores are strongest in near-OOD regimes, while geometry-aware scores such as NNGuide, fDBD, and CTM become more competitive as shift severity increases. On fine-tuned ViTs, the top cliques are led mainly by reconstruction- and residual-based scores. To interpret these ranking shifts, we analyze the last-layer representation using Neural Collapse (NC) metrics. The resulting picture is consistent across architectures: prototype- and boundary-aware scores become stronger when the representation is more collapsed and better aligned with classifier weights, whereas weaker-collapse regimes favor gradient- and manifold-based scores. Building on these insights, we propose two contributions: a simple PCA-based projection-filtering procedure that improves detector performance, and an approach that uses only the NC measurements of a trained classifier to predict its competitive out-of-distribution detector shortlist, without OOD data for that classifier and without knowledge of the shift.
